```{python}
#| echo: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import Markdown
from loguru import logger
from matplotlib.dates import DateFormatter, MonthLocator

import _chart_theme as theme
from realtime.settings import ARCHIVE_PATH

logger.disable("realtime")
theme.apply_chart_theme()

BYTES_PER_MEGABYTE = 1_000_000
file_size = f"{ARCHIVE_PATH.stat().st_size / BYTES_PER_MEGABYTE:.1f}"


def show_table(table: pd.DataFrame, decimals: int = 1) -> Markdown:
    """Shows a table of results in the page's own table style.

    Args:
        table: The table to show.
        decimals: The decimal places for numbers that are not whole.

    Returns:
        The table, ready to display.
    """
    rows = [
        [f"{value:.{decimals}f}" if isinstance(value, float) else str(value) for value in row]
        for row in table.itertuples(index=False)
    ]
    return Markdown(theme.markdown_table(list(table.columns), rows))
```

::: {.lead-text}
The archive consists of a single parquet file (currently `{python} file_size` MB.) The file is published as part of the site. You can download it, or point a query tool at its web address and read it from there.
:::

## Query the data without downloading the file

We recommend [DuckDB](https://duckdb.org/) for querying cuts of the data. [DuckDB](https://duckdb.org/) is a free database query engine that runs on your own computer and can read a parquet file from a web address.

The example query below asks for every value of UK GDP growth in the second quarter of 2020:

```sql
SELECT vintage_date::DATE AS published, value
FROM 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aeturrell/real-time-data/realtimedata.parquet'
WHERE series_id = 'IHYQ' AND reference_period = '2020Q2'
ORDER BY vintage_date
```

Another example: list every series, with its name and the dates of its first and latest publications:

```sql
SELECT
    series_id,
    any_value(title) AS title,
    min(vintage_date)::DATE AS first_published,
    max(vintage_date)::DATE AS latest_published
FROM 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aeturrell/real-time-data/realtimedata.parquet'
GROUP BY series_id
ORDER BY series_id
```

To run a query from the command line, [install DuckDB](https://duckdb.org/install/) and, if using from the command line, pass the query to it in quotes:

```bash
duckdb -c "
  SELECT vintage_date::DATE AS published, value
  FROM 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aeturrell/real-time-data/realtimedata.parquet'
  WHERE series_id = 'IHYQ' AND reference_period = '2020Q2'
  ORDER BY vintage_date"
```

You can also paste either query into [DuckDB's browser shell](https://shell.duckdb.org/) without installing anything. It works because the file's host sets CORS (cross-origin resource sharing), a permission that lets web pages on other sites read the file.

## Bulk download the file

```bash
curl -O https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aeturrell/real-time-data/realtimedata.parquet
```

## Explore the data

DuckDB also comes with a notebook-style interface, which is an easy way to browse the archive. It needs DuckDB 1.2.1 or later. If you already have **duckdb**, start the user interface with:

```bash
duckdb -ui
```

This opens the interface in your browser, installing the extension it needs on first run. In a notebook cell, make a view (a saved query you can treat as a table) of the file:

```sql
CREATE VIEW realtime AS
SELECT * FROM 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aeturrell/real-time-data/realtimedata.parquet'
```

Click `realtime` in the list on the left to see each column's type and a summary of its values, then write queries against it in further cells. The [DuckDB UI documentation](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/core_extensions/ui) covers the options, and [the announcement](https://duckdb.org/2025/03/12/duckdb-ui) of **DuckDB UI** gives a tour of its features.

## Use the data from Python

The rest of this page works from Python using [Ibis](https://ibis-project.org/), which writes queries that are executed by DuckDB. You'll need **DuckDB** and **Ibis** in your Python installation to run this. Run `uv add 'ibis-framework[duckdb]' pandas duckdb`.

Queries are ordinary Python code. Every example can be copied and run as it is.

```{python}
#| eval: false
import ibis
import pandas as pd
from ibis import _

archive = ibis.read_parquet("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aeturrell/real-time-data/realtimedata.parquet")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
import ibis
from ibis import _

archive = ibis.read_parquet(ARCHIVE_PATH)
```

In these examples, `_` stands for the table at that step of the query, so `_.value` means its `value` column.

## See the numbers as they stood on a past date

Here is the 2008 recession, as it looked at the end of January 2009 and as it looks now:

```{python}
KNOWN_ON = "2009-01-31"

known_then = _.vintage_date <= ibis.timestamp(KNOWN_ON)

recession = (
    archive.filter(
        _.series_id == "IHYQ",
        _.frequency == "Q",
        _.reference_period.between("2008Q1", "2008Q4"),
    )
    .group_by(quarter=_.reference_period)
    .agg(
        growth_then=_.value.argmax(_.vintage_date, where=known_then),
        growth_now=_.value.argmax(_.vintage_date),
    )
    .order_by("quarter")
    .to_pandas()
)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
then_total = recession["growth_then"].sum()
now_total = recession["growth_now"].sum()
show_table(
    recession.rename(
        columns={
            "quarter": "Quarter",
            "growth_then": "Growth known in January 2009 (%)",
            "growth_now": "Growth known now (%)",
        }
    )
)
```

Adding up the four quarters gives a rough sense of the difference: `{python} f"{then_total:.1f}"` percentage points as seen at the time, and `{python} f"{now_total:.1f}"` now. Anyone judging policy decisions from that winter should use the first column, because that is what people had in front of them.

## Examples

These are just illustrative.

### Follow a revision: unemployment

Unemployment rates are revised less than GDP growth, but they do change, sometimes in ways that alter the story. In October 2023 ONS stopped publishing its usual Labour Force Survey estimates, because too few people were responding. The survey returned in February 2024, reweighted to new population figures, and the data were reweighted again in December 2024.

This query collects each value of the unemployment rate (`MGSX`) with its publication date. The rates are rolling three-month figures, stored against the month each window ends.

```{python}
UNEMPLOYMENT_FROM = "2021-01"
UNEMPLOYMENT_TO = "2024-06"

unemployment = (
    archive.filter(
        _.series_id == "MGSX",
        _.frequency == "M",
        _.reference_period.between(UNEMPLOYMENT_FROM, UNEMPLOYMENT_TO),
    )
    .select(month=_.reference_period, vintage_date=_.vintage_date, value=_.value)
    .order_by("vintage_date")
    .to_pandas()
)


def unemployment_known_on(date: str) -> pd.Series:
    """Rebuilds the unemployment rate as it stood on a given date.

    Args:
        date: The date of interest.

    Returns:
        The latest rate known that day, for each month.
    """
    known = unemployment.loc[unemployment["vintage_date"] <= date]
    return known.groupby("month")["value"].last().sort_index()


before_pause = unemployment_known_on("2023-09-12")
after_return = unemployment_known_on("2024-02-13")
latest = unemployment.groupby("month")["value"].last().sort_index()
first_estimates = unemployment.groupby("month")["value"].first().sort_index()
```

```{python}

```

The February 2024 figures raised some earlier rates. For `{python} largest_change_month`, for example, the rate went from `{python} f"{largest_change_before:.1f}"`% to `{python} f"{largest_change_after:.1f}"`%. The later reweighting rewound some of that.

### Compare how much series get revised

Because all series share one format, a single query can compare them. This takes each period's first published value and its latest value, then measures the average gap. It leaves out `history` rows, because for those the archive does not hold the true first estimate. Recent periods have had less time to be revised, so these averages slightly understate the eventual gap.

```{python}
QUARTERLY_SERIES = ["IHYQ", "KG7P"]
MONTHLY_SERIES = ["ECYX", "IOP_MOM", "RSI_MOM", "MGSX"]

estimates = (
    archive.filter(
        (_.series_id.isin(QUARTERLY_SERIES) & (_.frequency == "Q"))
        | (_.series_id.isin(MONTHLY_SERIES) & (_.frequency == "M"))
    )
    .group_by(["series_id", "reference_period"])
    .agg(
        title=_.title.arbitrary(),
        first_estimate=_.value.argmin(_.vintage_date),
        latest_estimate=_.value.argmax(_.vintage_date),
        first_release_type=_.release_type.argmin(_.vintage_date),
    )
)

revision_sizes = (
    estimates.filter(_.first_release_type == "first")
    .mutate(revision=(_.latest_estimate - _.first_estimate).abs())
    .group_by("series_id")
    .agg(
        title=_.title.arbitrary(),
        periods=_.count(),
        average_revision=_.revision.mean(),
        largest_revision=_.revision.max(),
    )
    .order_by(ibis.desc("average_revision"))
    .to_pandas()
)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
show_table(
    revision_sizes.rename(
        columns={
            "series_id": "Series",
            "title": "Title",
            "periods": "Periods",
            "average_revision": "Average revision (points)",
            "largest_revision": "Largest revision (points)",
        }
    ),
    decimals=2,
)
```

### Trace a value back to its source

Every row records where the value came from, when it was fetched and a SHA-256 fingerprint of the original file. You can use the fingerprint to check that a copy of the file is the one used here.

```{python}
provenance = (
    archive.filter(
        _.series_id == "IHYQ",
        _.reference_period == "2020Q2",
        _.release_type == "first",
    )
    .select(
        _.value,
        published=_.vintage_date,
        source_url=_.source_url,
        retrieved=_.retrieved_at,
        content_sha256=_.content_sha256,
    )
    .to_pandas()
)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
FINGERPRINT_CHARACTERS_SHOWN = 12
source_row = provenance.iloc[0]
source_link = source_row["source_url"].removesuffix("/data")
fingerprint_start = source_row["content_sha256"][:FINGERPRINT_CHARACTERS_SHOWN]
```

The first estimate of `{python} f"{source_row['value']:.1f}"`% was published on `{python} f"{source_row['published']:%d %B %Y}"`. It came from [this page on the ONS website](`{python} source_link`){target="_blank" rel="noopener"}, and the fingerprint of the data behind it begins `{python} fingerprint_start`.

### An example nowcasting query

Of course, a major use case of real-time data is nowcasting. Below is an example that pulls quarterly GDP growth, monthly GDP, production, services, retail sales, unemployment, CPI inflation, and a business survey. All are growth rates, rates or scores, so their units do not shift between publications.

```{python}
NOWCASTING_SERIES = {
    "IHYQ": "Quarterly GDP growth",
    "ECYX": "Monthly GDP growth",
    "IOP_MOM": "Production growth",
    "IOS_MOM": "Services growth",
    "RSI_MOM": "Retail sales growth",
    "MGSX": "Unemployment rate",
    "D7G7": "CPI inflation",
    "AGENTS_CONSUMER_SERVICES_VALUES": "Agents' consumer services score",
}

quarterly_or_monthly = (_.series_id == "IHYQ").ifelse("Q", "M")

nowcasting_data = (
    archive.filter(
        _.series_id.isin(list(NOWCASTING_SERIES)),
        _.frequency == quarterly_or_monthly,
    )
    .select("vintage_date", "reference_period", "series_id", "value")
    .order_by(["vintage_date", "series_id", "reference_period"])
    .to_pandas()
)

nowcasting_data.head()
```

Those are the oldest rows, and `.tail()` gives the newest. To see what a model would have had on any date, keep the rows published by then and take the newest value for each series and period.

Next, let's pick a quarter and follow the data arriving between the day it began and the day of its first GDP estimate being released:

```{python}
CHOSEN_QUARTER = pd.Period("2025Q3", "Q")

first_gdp_estimate_date = nowcasting_data.loc[
    (nowcasting_data["series_id"] == "IHYQ")
    & (nowcasting_data["reference_period"] == str(CHOSEN_QUARTER)),
    "vintage_date",
].min()
months_in_quarter = pd.period_range(CHOSEN_QUARTER.start_time, CHOSEN_QUARTER.end_time, freq="M")

quarter_rows = nowcasting_data.loc[
    nowcasting_data["vintage_date"].between(CHOSEN_QUARTER.start_time, first_gdp_estimate_date)
].copy()
quarter_rows["about_chosen_quarter"] = quarter_rows["reference_period"].isin(
    [str(month) for month in months_in_quarter] + [str(CHOSEN_QUARTER)]
)
quarter_rows["chosen_quarter_period"] = quarter_rows["reference_period"].where(
    quarter_rows["about_chosen_quarter"], other=""
)

releases = (
    quarter_rows.groupby(["series_id", "vintage_date"])
    .agg(
        rows=("value", "size"),
        about_chosen_quarter=("about_chosen_quarter", "any"),
        newest_period=("chosen_quarter_period", "max"),
    )
    .reset_index()
)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-nowcast-flow
#| fig-cap: "Each dot is a day when new values were published for a series, from the start of the third quarter of 2025 up to its first GDP estimate. Bright dots carry a figure for the quarter itself, labelled with the month or quarter it describes. Grey dots carry only figures for other periods."
#| fig-alt: "A timeline with one row per series and publication dates running from July to November 2025. In the early months most series have only grey dots, for other periods. Bright dots labelled July, August and September appear as the quarter goes on. CPI inflation and retail sales report before monthly output. A vertical line marks the first GDP estimate in mid-November, the same day as the monthly GDP figure for September."
FLOW_FIGURE_SIZE = (8.6, 4.8)
DOT_SIZE = 42
LABEL_FONT_SIZE = 7
LABEL_LIFT = 0.2

series_rows = {series: row for row, series in enumerate(reversed(NOWCASTING_SERIES))}
new_information = releases.loc[releases["about_chosen_quarter"]]
older_information = releases.loc[~releases["about_chosen_quarter"]]


def period_label(period: str) -> str:
    """Shortens a period for a chart label, such as "2025-07" to "Jul".

    Args:
        period: The monthly or quarterly period.

    Returns:
        The label.
    """
    return f"Q{CHOSEN_QUARTER.quarter}" if "Q" in period else pd.Period(period, "M").strftime("%b")


figure, axes = plt.subplots(figsize=FLOW_FIGURE_SIZE, layout="constrained")
axes.scatter(
    older_information["vintage_date"],
    older_information["series_id"].map(series_rows),
    s=DOT_SIZE,
    color=theme.OXIDE_SLATE,
    label="Other periods only",
)
axes.scatter(
    new_information["vintage_date"],
    new_information["series_id"].map(series_rows),
    s=DOT_SIZE,
    color=theme.SCAN_LINE_CYAN,
    label="About the chosen quarter",
    zorder=3,
)
for release in new_information.itertuples():
    axes.annotate(
        period_label(release.newest_period),
        (release.vintage_date, series_rows[release.series_id] + LABEL_LIFT),
        ha="center",
        fontsize=LABEL_FONT_SIZE,
        color=theme.ELECTRON_WHITE,
    )
axes.axvline(first_gdp_estimate_date, color=theme.DEGAUSS_MAGENTA, label="First GDP estimate")
axes.set_yticks(list(series_rows.values()), [NOWCASTING_SERIES[series] for series in series_rows])
axes.xaxis.set_major_locator(MonthLocator())
axes.xaxis.set_major_formatter(DateFormatter("%b %Y"))
figure.legend(ncols=3, loc="outside lower center")
theme.add_chart_tag(axes, f"Data arriving for {CHOSEN_QUARTER}")
plt.show()

first_arrivals = (
    new_information.groupby("series_id")["vintage_date"].min().sort_values()
)
days_before_gdp = (first_gdp_estimate_date - first_arrivals).dt.days
earliest_series = first_arrivals.index[0]
```

The first GDP estimate came on `{python} f"{first_gdp_estimate_date:%d %B %Y}"`. The earliest signal about the quarter in this set was `{python} NOWCASTING_SERIES[earliest_series]`, `{python} f"{days_before_gdp.iloc[0]}"` days before that. A nowcast made partway through the quarter therefore has some series with figures for it and others that stop a month or two earlier. This uneven edge is what nowcasting models have to handle, and it is only visible with publication dates. Series can also skip a period: the archive holds no Agents' score for September 2025, and that score's dates are the latest it could have appeared, not exact days.

### Do business surveys lead GDP?

Surveys of firms, often called soft data, come out sooner than official GDP. They often provide a useful early signal.

This example uses two Bank of England Agents' scores, for consumer goods and consumer services, because they measure activity and have been public since 2006. Each is put on a common scale by subtracting its mean ($\mu$) and dividing by its standard deviation ($\sigma$):

$$
z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}
$$

The index is the average of the two over the latest three months.

For each quarter's GDP release, the code keeps only the rows published before that day, so nothing from the future leaks in.

```{python}
SURVEY_SERIES = ["AGENTS_CONSUMER_GOODS_VALUES", "AGENTS_CONSUMER_SERVICES_VALUES"]
RECENT_MONTHS = 3

survey_rows = (
    archive.filter(_.series_id.isin(SURVEY_SERIES))
    .select("series_id", "reference_period", "vintage_date", "value")
    .to_pandas()
)

gdp = (
    archive.filter(_.series_id == "IHYQ", _.frequency == "Q")
    .group_by(quarter=_.reference_period)
    .agg(
        first_estimate=_.value.argmin(_.vintage_date),
        latest_estimate=_.value.argmax(_.vintage_date),
        first_published=_.vintage_date.min(),
        first_release_type=_.release_type.argmin(_.vintage_date),
    )
    .filter(_.first_release_type == "first")
    .drop("first_release_type")
    .order_by("quarter")
    .to_pandas()
)
gdp.index = pd.PeriodIndex(gdp.pop("quarter"), freq="Q")
gdp = gdp.loc[gdp["first_published"] > survey_rows["vintage_date"].min()]


def survey_index_before(date: pd.Timestamp) -> float:
    """Builds the survey index from rows published before a given date.

    Args:
        date: The date of interest.

    Returns:
        The average standardised score over the latest months.
    """
    published = survey_rows.loc[survey_rows["vintage_date"] < date]
    scores = published.pivot_table(index="reference_period", columns="series_id", values="value")
    standardised = (scores - scores.mean()) / scores.std()
    return standardised.tail(RECENT_MONTHS).mean(axis=None)


gdp["survey_index"] = gdp["first_published"].map(survey_index_before)
```

The `survey_index` for a given quarter is what you could have worked out on the day before that quarter's first GDP estimate. It is compared with GDP growth in that quarter and the following ones. As a benchmark, the last column uses that day's first estimate of GDP instead of the survey index. (The pandemic and quarters from 2024 are left out.)

```{python}
PANDEMIC_QUARTERS = pd.period_range("2020Q1", "2021Q4", freq="Q")
SETTLED_BEFORE = pd.Period("2024Q1", "Q")
EARLIEST_QUARTER = gdp.index.min()
RECENT_START = pd.Period("2016Q1", "Q")
QUARTERS_AHEAD = range(4)


def correlations_ahead(
    quarters_ahead: int,
    start: pd.Period = EARLIEST_QUARTER,
    leave_out_pandemic: bool = True,
) -> dict[str, float | int]:
    """Measures how closely the survey index tracks GDP growth some quarters ahead.

    Args:
        quarters_ahead: How many quarters after the survey index to look.
        start: The earliest quarter of the survey index to use.
        leave_out_pandemic: Whether to drop pairs with either quarter in the pandemic.

    Returns:
        The correlations with the first and latest estimates, the benchmark
        correlation and the number of quarters compared.
    """
    pairs = gdp.assign(
        first_ahead=gdp["first_estimate"].shift(-quarters_ahead),
        latest_ahead=gdp["latest_estimate"].shift(-quarters_ahead),
    ).dropna()
    target_quarters = pairs.index + quarters_ahead
    keep = (target_quarters < SETTLED_BEFORE) & (pairs.index >= start)
    if leave_out_pandemic:
        keep = keep & ~pairs.index.isin(PANDEMIC_QUARTERS) & ~target_quarters.isin(PANDEMIC_QUARTERS)
    kept = pairs.loc[keep]
    return {
        "quarters_ahead": quarters_ahead,
        "with_first": kept["survey_index"].corr(kept["first_ahead"]),
        "with_latest": kept["survey_index"].corr(kept["latest_ahead"]),
        "gdp_alone": kept["first_estimate"].corr(kept["first_ahead"]),
        "quarters_compared": len(kept),
    }


correlations = pd.DataFrame([correlations_ahead(quarters) for quarters in QUARTERS_AHEAD])
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
SAME_QUARTER_BENCHMARK = "n/a"
table = correlations.astype({"gdp_alone": object})
table.loc[table["quarters_ahead"] == 0, "gdp_alone"] = SAME_QUARTER_BENCHMARK
show_table(
    table[["quarters_ahead", "with_first", "with_latest", "gdp_alone", "quarters_compared"]].rename(
        columns={
            "quarters_ahead": "Quarters ahead",
            "with_first": "Survey index and first estimate",
            "with_latest": "Survey index and latest estimate",
            "gdp_alone": "First GDP estimate alone",
            "quarters_compared": "Quarters compared",
        }
    ),
    decimals=2,
)
```

```{python}
#| fig-alt: "A line chart from 2006 with three lines in standard deviations: the survey index, first estimates of GDP growth and latest estimates of GDP growth. All three fall sharply in 2008 and 2009. The pandemic quarters are shaded and the lines run off the scale there. Each line is labelled at its right-hand end. In the other years the survey index moves more smoothly than GDP growth, and the two do not always move together."
SURVEY_FIGURE_SIZE = (8.6, 4.8)
Y_AXIS_MARGIN = 0.3
LABEL_DAYS_AFTER_END = 60
LABEL_MINIMUM_GAP = 0.75
LABEL_FONT_SIZE = 8
ONE_QUARTER = 1
PANDEMIC_SHADE_ALPHA = 0.25

quiet_quarters = gdp.loc[~gdp.index.isin(PANDEMIC_QUARTERS)]
first_on_scale = (gdp["first_estimate"] - quiet_quarters["first_estimate"].mean()) / quiet_quarters["first_estimate"].std()
latest_on_scale = (gdp["latest_estimate"] - quiet_quarters["latest_estimate"].mean()) / quiet_quarters["latest_estimate"].std()
survey_a_quarter_on = gdp["survey_index"].copy()
survey_a_quarter_on.index = survey_a_quarter_on.index + ONE_QUARTER

figure, axes = plt.subplots(figsize=SURVEY_FIGURE_SIZE, layout="constrained")
axes.axvspan(
    PANDEMIC_QUARTERS[0].start_time,
    PANDEMIC_QUARTERS[-1].end_time,
    color=theme.OXIDE_SLATE,
    alpha=PANDEMIC_SHADE_ALPHA,
)
survey_lines = [
    (survey_a_quarter_on, theme.PHOSPHOR_AMBER, "Survey index,\nknown a quarter earlier"),
    (first_on_scale, theme.SCAN_LINE_CYAN, "GDP growth:\nfirst estimate"),
    (latest_on_scale, theme.DEGAUSS_MAGENTA, "GDP growth:\nlatest estimate"),
]
outside_pandemic = pd.concat(
    [line.loc[~line.index.isin(PANDEMIC_QUARTERS)] for line, _colour, _label in survey_lines]
)
y_bottom = outside_pandemic.min() - Y_AXIS_MARGIN
y_top = outside_pandemic.max() + Y_AXIS_MARGIN
label_x = max(line.index.max() for line, _colour, _label in survey_lines).to_timestamp() + pd.Timedelta(days=LABEL_DAYS_AFTER_END)
label_y = None
for line, colour, label in sorted(survey_lines, key=lambda item: item[0].dropna().iloc[-1]):
    axes.plot(line.index.to_timestamp(), line, color=colour)
    end_value = line.dropna().iloc[-1]
    label_y = end_value if label_y is None else max(end_value, label_y + LABEL_MINIMUM_GAP)
    axes.text(label_x, label_y, label, color=colour, fontsize=LABEL_FONT_SIZE, va="center", clip_on=False)
axes.text(
    PANDEMIC_QUARTERS[0].start_time + (PANDEMIC_QUARTERS[-1].end_time - PANDEMIC_QUARTERS[0].start_time) / 2,
    y_top,
    "Pandemic",
    color=theme.SECONDARY_TEXT,
    fontsize=LABEL_FONT_SIZE,
    ha="center",
    va="bottom",
)
axes.set_ylim(y_bottom, y_top)
axes.set_ylabel("Standard deviations from mean")
theme.add_chart_tag(axes, "Survey index a quarter ahead of GDP")
plt.show()

one_ahead = correlations.loc[correlations["quarters_ahead"] == ONE_QUARTER].iloc[0]
one_ahead_recent = correlations_ahead(ONE_QUARTER, start=RECENT_START)
one_ahead_with_pandemic = correlations_ahead(ONE_QUARTER, leave_out_pandemic=False)
```

The survey index gives a modest early signal: one quarter ahead, its correlation with the first estimate is `{python} f"{one_ahead['with_first']:.2f}"`. The index pulls ahead three quarters out.
